notable_absence.finding: (1) No edition statement anywhere, even though this is a feature with a control bit and a dedicated role, and two other pages in this module carry bold EE admonitions. A reader cannot tell from this page whether sequential scans exist in Community Edition. (2) No `availableSince`, though sequential scans are a comparatively recent feature (7.6) and the page's own explain-plan and completed-requests output would differ on older releases. The `n1qlFeatCtrl` value `76` appears twice as a worked example with no statement of which release's default it is, so the arithmetic in Examples 5 and 6 is only reproducible on whatever version the author had. (3) No state or enum vocabulary at all, so this page contributes nothing to the state-vocabulary question - except negatively: its sample output contains `"scanConsistency": "unbounded"`, a value that is not in the promoted `n1ql:scan-consistency` enum, matching the same wrong spelling on storage-modes.md. (4) The `~qualifier` mechanism is described as automatic with a 10000-key threshold and the threshold is never said to be configurable or not. (5) The page never says what a sequential scan costs or how it scales, beyond 'Notice that the query takes one or more seconds' for 11 documents - which is a striking number to publish without comment. (6) No mention of whether a sequential scan can be used for anything other than retrieving document keys, i.e. whether predicates are pushed down; the first sentence says the fallback retrieves 'the document keys' and the plan then shows a Fetch operator, which implies no pushdown, but the page never states it.

cross_component_finding: (1) A SENTENCE THAT CONTRADICTS THE PAGE'S PREMISE. The 'Use Sequential Scans' section opens: 'To query an index using sequential scan, run the query as usual.' There is no index - that is the entire subject of the page, and two sections later the page says so explicitly ('This name is a placeholder — in reality there is no index'). The instruction should be to query a keyspace, or a collection. (2) FOUR SPELLINGS OF ONE SETTING, IN ONE TABLE. Table 1's 'Name of option' column reads **N1QL Feature Controller** (UI), --n1ql-feature-control (CLI), queryN1QLFeatCtrl (cluster REST), n1ql-feat-ctrl (node REST). Four surfaces, four names, no statement that they are one setting other than the table's own caption; and the sample completed-requests output uses a fifth spelling, `n1qlFeatCtrl`, as the field name. This is the same defect shape as the scan-consistency naming problem elsewhere in the module, and it is worse here because the setting is a bitmask, so a user who finds the wrong name and sets it to `16384` rather than to the OR of the current value will silently clear every other feature bit. (3) THE OFF/ON PROCEDURES ARE ASYMMETRIC AND FRAGILE. Switching off uses bitwise OR; switching on uses bitwise XOR. XOR is not the inverse of OR: applying the documented 'switch on' procedure to a value where the bit is already clear will SET it, i.e. switch the feature off. The correct inverse is AND NOT. The worked examples conceal this because they run OR then XOR on the same value (76 -> 16460 -> 76), which round-trips only because the first step actually changed the bit. A reader who runs Example 6 on a system where sequential scans are already on will turn them off. (4) The role's own name is stated in bold prose twice and never linked to its reference page, while the generic 'Authorization' overview is linked instead - so the one place a reader could confirm the role's exact name and scope is not linked from the page that requires it. (5) Table 1's cross-reference anchor is '[Table 1](#n1ql-feat-ctrl)', which is the CLI/REST option name rather than a table id, and the table itself is rendered as bold text ('__Table 1. How to get or set the N1QL Feature Controller__') rather than as a captioned table, so the anchor has no target in the Markdown snapshot.
cross_product_finding: cloud/indexes/query-without-index.json already covers the Capella version of this page and used `privilege:query-use-sequential-scans`, an id the registry now aliases to promoted `role:query-use-sequential-scans` after round 12 re-filed eleven such ids. This Server page settles that question in the corpus's favour by calling it a role, in bold, twice - so the alias can be treated as a documented correction rather than a reconciliation guess, and phase 2 can retire the `privilege:` spelling for this term with a citation. The second cross-product note is the `data:kv-range-scan` / `sdk:kv-range-scan` pair: both ids exist in the corpus, both were minted from the phrase 'range scan', and they are not the same thing - the SDK id names a client API family (documented in the SDK trees), this one names the Data Service mechanism the Query Service uses internally. They will look like a namespace fork to any tool that compares suffixes, and they are not one. Third: the whole Manage Sequential Scans section is Server-only in substance, because its four configuration surfaces include a CLI and a node-level REST endpoint that a Capella user has no access to; a cross-product merge of `index:sequential-scan` will therefore find `configurableVia` relations on the Server side with no Capella counterpart, for product-shape reasons rather than feature differences.
